title: Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP/1.1): Semantics and Content
summary: Defines what HTTP/1.1 messages mean: request methods, header fields, response status codes, payload handling, and content negotiation. It is one of the documents that replaced RFC 2616. It was later replaced by RFC 9110.

eli5.summary: This explains what words like GET and POST mean when your browser talks to a website, and what the website's answers mean. It has since been replaced by a newer version.

questions: what do http status codes mean
what is the difference between put and post
what are safe and idempotent http methods
what does http 301 vs 302 vs 307 mean
subtitle: What HTTP/1.1 requests and responses actually mean: methods, status codes, headers and content negotiation.

tldr.problem: HTTP needs a shared meaning for what a client is asking for and what a server's answer means, whatever kind of resource sits behind the URL.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7231 defines representations and metadata, content negotiation, eight request methods, request and response header fields, and the five classes of three-digit status codes.
tldr.outcome: It replaced the semantics half of RFC 2616 and has itself been obsoleted by RFC 9110, so it is a historical reference rather than the current definition.

facts.label: Methods defined
facts.value: 8: GET, HEAD, POST, PUT, DELETE, CONNECT, OPTIONS, TRACE

facts.label: Quality value range
facts.value: 0 to 1, up to three decimal digits

today: RFC 7231 has been obsoleted by RFC 9110, which is now the place to read HTTP semantics. It replaced the semantics part of RFC 2616 and updated RFC 2817, and its Appendix B lists what changed from RFC 2616.

sections.title: What This Document Covers
sections.content:
Each HTTP message is either a request or a response. A server parses each request, interprets it against the identified request target, and answers with one or more response messages. RFC 7231 defines those request and response semantics on top of the message architecture of RFC 7230.

The semantics have four parts: the intent of each request method, extensions carried by request header fields, the meaning of status codes, and the meaning of response header fields. The document also defines representation metadata and the selection algorithms collectively called content negotiation. Conditional requests, range requests, caching and authentication are split out into RFC 7232, RFC 7233, RFC 7234 and RFC 7235.
sections.eli5: This is the part of the web rulebook that says what each request and answer means, like a dictionary for a conversation between your browser and a website.

sections.title: Resources and Representations
sections.content:
The target of a request is a resource, identified by a URI. HTTP does not limit what a resource can be; it only defines an interface for interacting with it. One design goal is to separate resource identification from request semantics. If the method semantics conflict with a meaning implied by the URI itself, the method semantics take precedence.

Clients never touch a resource directly. They exchange representations: information reflecting a past, current or desired state of the resource, made of representation metadata plus a potentially unbounded stream of representation data. The Content-Type field names the media type, for example text/html; charset=ISO-8859-4. The Content-Encoding field lists content codings such as gzip, in the order they were applied, so the data is modelled as Content-Encoding(Content-Type(bits)). Content-Language and Content-Location complete the metadata.

If Content-Type is missing, a recipient may assume application/octet-stream or examine the data. The RFC warns that such content sniffing can expose security risks and encourages a way to disable it.
sections.eli5: A website cannot hand you the thing itself, so it sends you a picture of it, like a photo of a toy. Labels on the photo tell you the type of file and whether it is squished to save space.

sections.title: Content Negotiation
sections.content:
A server may have the same information in several formats, languages or encodings. HTTP supports two visible patterns. In proactive (server-driven) negotiation the client states its preferences and the server picks. In reactive (agent-driven) negotiation the server sends a list of alternatives, for example in a 300 or 406 response, and the client chooses.

Proactive preferences travel in Accept, Accept-Charset, Accept-Encoding and Accept-Language. Each can carry a weight, the q parameter, from 0 to 1 with at most three digits after the decimal point. A value of 0 means not acceptable, and the default is 1. When several media ranges match, the most specific one wins, so text/plain;format=flowed beats text/plain, which beats text/*, which beats */*.

The RFC is frank about the costs of proactive negotiation: the server cannot know what is really best, describing capabilities in every request is inefficient and a privacy risk, and it limits reuse of responses by shared caches. A Vary response field tells caches and clients which request fields influenced the choice.
sections.eli5: It is like ordering at a restaurant. You can tell the waiter your favourites up front, or the waiter can hand you a menu and let you choose.

sections.title: Request Methods
sections.content:
The method token is the primary source of request semantics and is case-sensitive. This document defines eight: GET, HEAD, POST, PUT, DELETE, CONNECT, OPTIONS and TRACE. All general-purpose servers MUST support GET and HEAD; every other method is optional. An unrecognized method should get 501, and a known method that the resource does not allow should get 405 with an Allow header.

Two properties matter most. A safe method is essentially read-only, which lets spiders and prefetching work without harm: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE. An idempotent method has the same intended effect whether sent once or many times: PUT, DELETE and the safe methods. Idempotence lets a client retry automatically after a connection failure.

PUT creates or replaces the target's state, answering 201 when it creates and 200 or 204 when it modifies. POST asks the resource to process the payload by its own rules, and a server that creates a resource SHOULD answer 201 with a Location header. CONNECT asks a proxy to open a tunnel, and proxies SHOULD restrict it to known ports. A server MUST NOT send validators such as ETag in a successful PUT response unless the stored data is identical to what was sent.
sections.eli5: Methods are verbs. GET means please show me, PUT means put this there, and DELETE means take it away. Some verbs are safe because they only look, and asking twice does no extra harm.

sections.title: Response Status Codes
sections.content:
A status code is a three-digit result. The first digit gives the class, and a client MUST understand the class even for an unknown code, treating it like the x00 code of that class. For example, an unrecognized 471 is handled as 400, and a response with an unrecognized code MUST NOT be cached.

Notable codes include 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content, 301 Moved Permanently, 302 Found, 303 See Other, 307 Temporary Redirect, 404 Not Found, 410 Gone, 405 Method Not Allowed, 415 Unsupported Media Type and 503 Service Unavailable. The reason phrases are only recommendations.

On redirects, history shows through: early clients split over whether 301 and 302 keep the method, so this document allows a user agent to change POST to GET for those two, while 307 forbids changing the method. The 305 code is deprecated and 306 is reserved. The Expect: 100-continue mechanism lets a client with a large body ask for an interim 100 (Continue) before sending it.
sections.eli5: Status codes are like traffic lights for answers. Starting with 2 means all good, 3 means go somewhere else, 4 means you made a mistake, and 5 means the website broke.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC notes that most HTTP semantics concerns are about securing server applications and user agent processing rather than the protocol itself. It lists several specific risks.

  • File and path names: servers must avoid special names such as .. when mapping request targets to files.
  • Injection: any request element can carry data misread as a command or query, such as SQL injection through Host or Referer.
  • Sensitive data in URIs: URIs are shared, not secured, so sensitive form data should use POST rather than GET.
  • Fragments after redirects: a fragment inherited through Location can disclose one site's fragment to another.
  • Product information and fingerprinting: User-Agent, Server and detailed Accept-Charset lists can reveal or identify software and users.
sections.eli5: Be careful what you put in the address, because addresses get seen by many people. And never trust what strangers send to your website without checking it first.

viz.caption: THE FIVE STATUS CODE CLASSES (RFC 7231, SECTION 6)

items.label: Informational
items.desc: The request was received, continuing process.

items.label: Successful
items.desc: The request was successfully received, understood, and accepted.

items.label: Redirection
items.desc: Further action needs to be taken in order to complete the request.

items.label: Client Error
items.desc: The request contains bad syntax or cannot be fulfilled.

items.label: Server Error
items.desc: The server failed to fulfill an apparently valid request.

messages.label: PUT with Expect: 100-continue
messages.note: Request line and header fields only, for a large body.

messages.label: 100 (Continue)
messages.note: Or an immediate final status such as 401 or 405 if the headers already decide it.

messages.label: Final status code
messages.note: A server that sent 100 MUST ultimately send a final status.
